facts.head: origin/ju26-issue-2297
facts.commitMessage: implement issue #2297 : Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code
riskReasons: large generated/snapshot churn hides the real diff
changes code-generation templates (every consumer is affected)

summary: The change adds a guarded [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] attribute to the type declarations in six T4 templates (and their generated .cs). It also fixes a missing newline after a nesting-type brace, adds a README note and two new tests, and regenerates about 222 snapshot files. The guard makes the attribute apply only on targets other than netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework.

requirementItems.text: Every type the generator emits (object formatters, string-key formatters, enum formatters, union formatters, resolver, composite resolver, nested helper classes) is decorated with `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute`.
Generated code still compiles on every target the generator supports, including targets where the attribute type or its applicability differs (netstandard2.0, .NET Framework).
Verified snapshot files are updated to match the new output, with no other differences.
No run-time behaviour change in serialization.
No unrelated dependency or build changes.

claims.statement: Object (int-key) formatter, string-key formatter, enum formatter and union formatter templates each emit [global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] directly before the 'internal sealed class' declaration.
ResolverTemplate emits the attribute on the resolver partial class and on both nested helper classes (FormatterCache<T> and <Resolver>GetFormatterHelper).
CompositeResolverTemplate emits the attribute on the composite resolver partial class and its nested FormatterCache<T> class.
No type emitted by any generator template lacks the attribute (including any other emitted types or templates, e.g. nested/array/generic helper types, not touched by this diff).

Each attribute is wrapped in '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK ... #endif', so generated code compiles for consumers targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework; on those targets coverage exclusion is simply absent.
The .cs files under Transforms are edited by hand or regenerated consistently with the .tt files, so each .tt change has an identical counterpart in its .cs file.

Scope: TransformUtilities.EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces changes its opening brace output from '{' to '{\r\n' when the nesting type has type constraints; this changes generated output for nested constrained types and no requirement asks for it.

Scope: the README gains a paragraph promising that all generated formatters and resolvers carry [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] except on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework. The requirements do not ask for documentation.

The new test AllGeneratedTypesAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage proves every generated file in a sample compilation contains the attribute. It checks only file-level presence with string Contains, not that each type is decorated, and not for nested helper classes, composite resolvers, or generic or constrained types.

The test ExcludeAttributeIsGuardedForTargetsWhereItIsUnavailable proves every attribute occurrence is wrapped by the #if guard. It does not compile the output against netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework.
The roughly 222 regenerated snapshot files differ from their previous versions only by the added guarded attribute lines and the brace newline fix, with no other differences.
Non-change: the generated serialization and deserialization method bodies, and the formatter lookup logic, are unchanged. Only attributes, preprocessor lines and whitespace are added.
Non-change: no csproj, package reference, build props or public API files are modified.

verdicts.reasoning: I grepped all .tt files for ExcludeFromCodeCoverage and NETSTANDARD2_0. The two named files hold 4 attribute occurrences, each wrapped by the same '#if' / '#endif' pair. evidence.note: ExcludeFromCodeCoverage occurrence counts match between each .tt and its .cs: Composite 2/2, Resolver 3/3, Enum 1/1, Union 1/1, Formatter 1/1, StringKey 1/1.

The three .tt insertions (resolver class, FormatterCache, GetFormatterHelper) each appear as the same `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` / attribute / `#endif` text in the Write string literals, using \r\n and the same tab indentation.

#endif

This hand-written helper has no .tt counterpart. Its `{` to `{\r\n` change applies only to nesting types with constraints, so it is not covered by this claim. It is a separate behaviour change that affects generated output.

verdicts.reasoning: I compared each .tt hunk with its .cs hunk. Every .tt insertion has an equivalent in the .cs Write call, with the same condition, attribute text and indentation. The .cs files have no extra attribute insertions beyond the .tt ones. I could not run the T4 transform, so I cannot confirm the .cs files are byte-identical to what the generator would emit. verdicts.basis: Direct code reading of the whole method at HEAD plus the diff hunk. No execution and no snapshot comparison.

evidence.note: At HEAD the opening brace is written as `anyConstraints ? "{\r\n" : " {\r\n"`. The diff shows the base wrote `"{"` with no newline in the constrained case.

EmitTypeConstraints returns true only when a type parameter has constraints. It then writes each `where` clause ending in `\r\n`. So the changed branch applies only to nesting types that have constrained generic parameters.

verdicts.reasoning: The diff contains the change described in the claim. In the constrained case the brace now ends with a newline, so generated text for nested generic types with constraints differs. That output is whitespace only: the next emitted text now starts on a new line instead of following `{` on the same line. The requirement covers only adding ExcludeFromCodeCoverage, and F3 says snapshots should have no other differences. Neither F1, F2 nor F3 asks for a brace or line-ending change. The likely motive is that an attribute line is now emitted right after the brace, but I did not verify that. I also did not check whether any snapshot has a nested constrained type. The human decides whether this is acceptable.

evidence.note: The test asserts at least 5 generated files. For each file it only checks `text.Contains(ExcludeAttribute)`. It does not count the attribute per type or per declaration.

The sample source has only a non-generic int-keyed object, a string-keyed object, an enum, a union with one member, and a `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` partial class. It has no generic or constrained types and no composite resolver setup. Nothing in the test targets nested helper classes.

verdicts.reasoning: The test does check that every generated file contains the attribute string, which is the positive part of the claim. It uses file-level string Contains only, so one decorated type would satisfy a file that holds several types. The sample covers none of the cases the claim lists as missing: generic or constrained types, composite resolvers, and nested helper classes. The second test, ExcludeAttributeIsGuardedForTargetsWhereItIsUnavailable, counts attribute occurrences against guarded occurrences. It does not compare either count to the number of emitted types, so it does not close the per-type gap.

RunGeneratorAsync only runs the generator through CSharpGeneratorDriver and reads the generated text. It never emits or checks diagnostics of the output, and the references come from DefaultTargetFrameworkReferences. So nothing is compiled against netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework.
The emitted text is `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK\r\n\t[...ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]\r\n#endif`, which matches the shape the test looks for after CRLF is normalised.

verdicts.reasoning: The test compares the total attribute count with the wrapped count for every generated file in its sample. That supports the first half of the claim, within the sample: integer-key, string-key, enum and union formatters plus the resolver. The test is text-only, so the second half is also true. The "every" is limited to the sample source. Template variants the sample does not trigger are not covered, such as the composite resolver and generic or nested helper classes. The test also checks only that the guard string is present. It does not check that the guard condition is correct for the real targets.
